title: Causal inference | Embeddings & RAG
objectives: Choose and defend a quasi-experimental method when you cannot randomise. Build a working retrieval-augmented generation pipeline.
exercise: Re-analyse a past non-randomised launch from work with DiD and write up the assumptions. Build a RAG bot over 30–50 public fintech policy documents (e.g. a central bank's or payments regulator's FAQs) using DuckDB/FAISS plus any LLM API.
resources: Matheus Facure, Causal Inference for the Brave and True (free, Python)
Hugging Face Agents Course, Unit 3 (agentic RAG)

units.concepts: Parallel trends, event studies, staggered adoption

units.title: Hybrid search & reranking

cards.q: Why does comparing users who adopted a feature with those who didn't overstate its effect?
cards.answer: Self-selection: adopters differ systematically (more engaged, higher intent, power users). They would have had better outcomes even without the feature. The naive difference = true effect + selection bias (E[Y₀|adopt] − E[Y₀|not adopt] > 0).

cards.q: The fundamental problem of causal inference is…
choices: We never observe both potential outcomes Y(1) and Y(0) for the same unit

cards.q: ATT is…
choices: The average effect among those who actually received treatment
The average effect across the whole population

cards.q: Why does randomisation remove selection bias?
choices: Assignment is independent of potential outcomes, so groups are comparable in expectation

cards.q: Naive difference in means equals…
Should you control for a variable caused by both treatment and outcome?
choices: No: it's a collider; conditioning opens a spurious path

cards.q: A confounder is…
choices: A common cause of treatment and outcome
A variable on the causal path from treatment to outcome
A common effect of treatment and outcome

cards.q: Promo → app opens → purchases. Estimating the total effect of the promo on purchases, should you control for app opens?
choices: No: it's a mediator; controlling removes part of the effect you want

cards.q: You analyse only approved loans and find income unrelated to default. Why might that mislead?
choices: Selection on approval (a collider of income and risk) induces bias

cards.q: The backdoor criterion asks you to…
choices: Block all non-causal paths from treatment to outcome without conditioning on descendants of treatment

cards.q: State the parallel-trends assumption and one way to check it.
cards.answer: Without treatment, the treated and control groups' outcomes would have moved in parallel (same trend). Check: plot pre-period trends, or run an event study with leads (pre-treatment coefficients should be ≈ 0). Also run placebo tests on fake treatment dates.
rubric: Pre-trend plot / event-study leads / placebo test

cards.q: Treated region: 100 → 130. Control region: 80 → 95. What is the DiD estimate?
In the regression Y = β0 + β1·Treated + β2·Post + β3·(Treated×Post), the DiD effect is…
Known problem with two-way fixed-effects DiD under staggered adoption?
choices: Already-treated units act as controls, which can bias the estimate when effects vary over time; use modern estimators (e.g. Callaway–Sant'Anna)
It can't handle more than two periods

cards.q: A concurrent marketing campaign hit only the treated region. What does this break?
choices: Parallel trends (no other shocks differ between groups)

cards.q: A feature launched globally with no holdout. Which method could estimate its impact?
choices: Synthetic control / interrupted time series (using pre-period trends and unaffected comparison series)

cards.q: A valid instrument Z must…
choices: Affect treatment (relevance) and affect the outcome only through treatment (exclusion), unconfounded
Be correlated with the outcome directly

cards.q: Credit limits jump at score 700. Which design fits?
cards.explain: Compare users just above vs just below; the estimate is local to the cutoff.

cards.q: In an encouragement design (random nudge to adopt), IV estimates…
choices: The LATE: the effect for compliers whose adoption was changed by the nudge

cards.q: Propensity-score matching relies on which key assumption?
choices: No unmeasured confounding (conditional ignorability) plus overlap

cards.q: Why use cosine similarity rather than raw dot product with unnormalised embeddings?
choices: Dot product rewards vector length (magnitude), not just direction; cosine compares direction only

cards.q: A text embedding is…
choices: A dense vector where semantically similar texts are close

cards.q: Cosine similarity of a = (1, 0) and b = (1, 1)? (3 dp)
You switch embedding models. What must you do?
choices: Re-embed the whole corpus: vectors from different models aren't comparable

cards.q: Why do vector databases use approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes like HNSW?
choices: Exact search over millions of vectors is too slow; ANN trades a little recall for big speedups

cards.q: What breaks when chunks are too small? Too large?
cards.answer: Too small: chunks lose context (a definition is split from its conditions), retrieval returns fragments, and you need many chunks. Too large: embeddings average several topics, which dilutes similarity. Irrelevant text eats context and cost, and precision drops.
rubric: Large → diluted embeddings, lower precision, more tokens

cards.q: Why add overlap between consecutive chunks?
choices: So information near boundaries isn't split across chunks

cards.q: For regulatory FAQs with clear Q/A sections, the best chunking is…
choices: Structure-aware: one Q/A pair or section per chunk, with its heading

cards.q: Why attach metadata (source, section, date) to chunks?
choices: For filtering (e.g. latest policy only), citations and debugging

cards.q: Contextual chunk headers / contextual retrieval means…
choices: Prepending document/section context to each chunk before embedding so it stands alone

cards.q: Which query type does BM25 handle better than dense retrieval?
choices: Exact identifiers and rare terms (e.g. 'MAS Notice 626', error codes)

cards.q: Hybrid search typically combines rankings via…
choices: Reciprocal rank fusion (or weighted score fusion) of BM25 and dense results
Taking only the BM25 top hit

cards.q: A cross-encoder reranker…
choices: Scores each (query, document) pair jointly: more accurate but too slow for the full corpus, so it reranks the top-k
Embeds the query and documents separately

cards.q: Query rewriting helps when…
choices: User queries are vague, conversational ('what about for that?') or use different terms from the documents

cards.q: Which metric measures 'did the right document appear in the top 5'?
The correct document was retrieved, but the answer is wrong. Retrieval or generation failure?
cards.explain: Fix it with prompting, grounding instructions, a better model, or fewer distracting chunks.

cards.q: The answer cites a policy that isn't in any retrieved chunk. This is…
When can long context replace RAG?
choices: Small, stable corpora that fit comfortably in context, where cost/latency is acceptable
cards.explain: Large or fast-changing corpora, permissions, and cost still favour retrieval.

cards.q: Agentic RAG differs from basic RAG in that…
choices: The model decides when/what to retrieve, can reformulate and retrieve iteratively

cards.q: The assistant answers from a 2023 fee schedule when a 2026 one exists. Best fix?
choices: Metadata filtering/recency boosting and removing superseded documents from the index
